learn.title: One program, many files
learn.body: Real programs are split across files. Each `.c` file is compiled to its own `.o`, then the linker joins them. If you change one file, only that one needs compiling again.

learn.title: twice.c
learn.body: The definition of `twice`. It includes its own header to stay consistent.

learn.title: main.c
learn.body: `main` includes the header and calls `twice`. Together with `twice.h` from the last lesson it prints 42.

learn.title: Build by hand
learn.body: Compile each file, link the objects, run.
learn.code:
cc -c main.c
cc -c twice.c
cc main.o twice.o -o prog
./prog

learn.title: A Makefile
learn.body: `make` reads rules: a target, a colon, what it depends on, then a command. The commands must start with a tab, not spaces (shown here as spaces).
learn.code:
prog: main.o twice.o
    cc main.o twice.o -o prog
main.o: main.c twice.h
    cc -c main.c
twice.o: twice.c twice.h
    cc -c twice.c

learn.title: What make does
steps: `main.o` is up to date, so it is skipped
It relinks `prog`; a second `make` says it is up to date

learn.body: For one file, `make hello` builds `hello` from `hello.c` with no Makefile at all.

questions.explanation: `-c` stops before linking, so you get an object file.

questions.prompt: Put the manual build in order.
steps: Link main.o and twice.o into prog
questions.explanation: Both objects must exist before the linker can join them.

questions.prompt: What program reads a Makefile and rebuilds only what changed? Type its name.
questions.explanation: `make` compares file times and runs only the needed commands.

questions.prompt: You change only `twice.c`. What does `make` recompile?
questions.explanation: `main.o` is still up to date, so it is skipped.

questions.prompt: Each command line in a real Makefile must start with a \_\_ character.
questions.explanation: `make` insists on a tab there, which is a common trap.

questions.prompt: What does the line `prog: main.o twice.o` mean?
questions.explanation: Before the colon is the target, after it are the things it depends on.

questions.prompt: Why split a program into several files?
choices: Changing one file means recompiling only that file
The linker is not needed then
questions.explanation: Splitting also keeps related code together and easier to read.
